scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

You may be more likely to act in ways that align with the community's values and norms in order to maintain social bonds and avoid social disapproval. 5. **Limited exposure to alternative perspectives**: While being part of a close-knit community can provide a sense of comfort and security, it can also limit your exposure to alternative perspectives and ideas. This might lead to a more narrow or insular view of the world, which can influence how you think about right and wrong. 6. **Spiritual growth and development**: On the other hand, being part of a religious community can also facilitate spiritual growth and development, which can, in turn, influence your moral compass. As you engage with your community and reflect on your faith, you may develop a deeper understanding of yourself and the world around you. prediction.raw: 0. The scenario you've described suggests that you are not in the wrong (NTA) for refusing to pump your girlfriend's tire. Here's why: 1. **You've already helped and educated her**: You previously noticed the issue with her tire, informed her, and even took the initiative to buy her a PSI gauge and show her how to use it. This demonstrates that you've been supportive and willing to help her learn basic car maintenance. 2. **You've set clear boundaries**: You've made it clear that your capabilities with car maintenance are limited to the basics and that you prefer a mechanic to handle more complex issues. This is a reasonable boundary, especially considering you've already taken steps to empower her with the knowledge to handle simple tasks like checking tire pressure. 3. **Her expectations are unreasonable and rooted in outdated gender roles**: Her insistence that it's a man's responsibility to handle such tasks, and her reliance on strangers (specifically men) to do things she's capable of learning, suggests an unhealthy dynamic. Her refusal to learn and take responsibility for her own car maintenance, coupled with her expectation that you should take on this role solely because you're a man, is not only unfair but also perpetuates harmful gender stereotypes. 4. **You contribute significantly to the relationship**: You've mentioned that you do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly, and pay the majority of your expenses. This indicates that you're a contributing and supportive partner, which further supports the notion that your refusal to pump her tire is not about being unhelpful or unmanly, but about standing against unfair expectations and promoting mutual responsibility and respect. 5. **Her refusal to learn and grow**: Despite your offer to show her how to use the pump again, she refused. This refusal, combined with her previous actions and expectations, suggests a lack of willingness to take responsibility for her own needs and learn new skills, which is an important aspect of personal growth and independence. In summary, your decision to refuse pumping her tire, given the context and the dynamics at play, seems justified. It's about setting boundaries, promoting mutual respect, and challenging outdated gender roles that can be harmful to both parties in a relationship.
